code.originalText: Two-week review of lung function and blood tests, diagnosis, start of treatment, and pulmonology consultation

text.paragraph: Two-week review of lung function and blood tests; pulmonology consultation today. [S]

Mr. Locke returns two weeks after his first visit. He has used albuterol once or twice a day, and not since early this morning, six hours before his tests. The open fires in his rooms have not been lit since his first visit; the household has put electric heaters in his study and bedroom, and a HEPA air cleaner runs in each. He has stayed in the country and checks the air quality index each morning. His night cough has eased to two nights a week, but he is still breathless on stairs and hills and wheezes in the cold. He has had no fever, weight loss, night sweats, or blood in his sputum. This morning he had full lung function tests, a six-minute walk, and a CT of the chest, and saw Dr. Nwankwo-Fairfax of pulmonology. [S]

list.item:
Asthma with persistent airflow limitation, type 2 phenotype (J45.40). Before bronchodilator, FEV1 2.11 L (62 percent predicted) and FEV1/FVC 0.57; after albuterol, FEV1 2.49 L, a rise of 380 mL (11 percent of predicted, a positive response by the ATS/ERS 1688 criterion), with FEV1/FVC 0.62, still below the lower limit of normal (0.67) and below 0.70: airflow limitation that is partly reversible but persists after bronchodilator. FeNO 41 ppb, blood eosinophils 0.46 x 10^3/uL, and IgE 186 IU/mL show type 2 airway inflammation; DLCO 26.4 is normal and the CT shows bronchial wall thickening and air trapping without emphysema or bronchiectasis. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is normal, the interferon-gamma release assay is negative, NT-proBNP is normal, and the chest X-ray is clear. COPD from non-tobacco exposures was considered, because GOLD recognizes COPD in never-smokers exposed to air pollution and solid-fuel smoke and his post-bronchodilator ratio is below 0.70. The features favor asthma: symptoms from his late thirties that vary with season, cold, and smoke, a large bronchodilator response, raised FeNO and eosinophils, no emphysema, and a normal DLCO. The persistent limitation is best explained by long-standing asthma, with pollution and indoor smoke as aggravating causes. Dr. Nwankwo-Fairfax agrees. Because GINA and GOLD advise that anyone with asthma features be treated as asthma, inhaled corticosteroid is essential and a long-acting bronchodilator alone is not safe. [S]
Budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg, two inhalations twice daily and one as needed, no more than 12 a day (GINA track 1, step 4), starting today.
Stop albuterol.
Inhaler technique taught with his own device and checked by teach-back.
Written asthma action plan given; home peak flow twice daily to find his personal best.
Pulmonary rehabilitation program, eight weeks, starting next week.
Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine PCV20 today.
Review in twelve weeks with repeat spirometry and FeNO.

Chronic cough with wheeze and breathlessness (R05.3). Explained by asthma with persistent airflow limitation; superseded by that diagnosis. Tuberculosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, heart failure, and a tumor are excluded. [S]
Managed under the asthma problem.

Exposure to air pollution and indoor solid-fuel smoke (Z77.110). Removing the open fires is the largest change within his control. Fine particles from coal, wood, and traffic aggravate asthma and add to airflow limitation; the WHO 1687 guideline values for PM2.5 are 5 ug/m3 as an annual mean and 15 ug/m3 over 24 hours. [S]
Keep the open fires out of use; HEPA air cleaners in his study and bedroom.
Check the air quality index each morning; on days of 101 or more (unhealthy for sensitive groups) avoid outdoor exertion and postpone city trips.
A well-fitted N95 respirator for unavoidable time outdoors on alert days; walk away from main roads.
